title: The naive framing: "you'd need formulas"
text: People assume understanding a year of revenue means learning spreadsheet formulas. It doesn't. You just ask in plain English. So, it's actually sitting in that file you never open.

title: Why the spreadsheet stays closed
text: Solo operators often avoid their own numbers. A folder called finances, 12 months of revenue inside it, never opened because opening it means formulas and formulas mean guessing its syntax and still not trusting the answer. Without help, understanding your numbers looks like a loop. Export a CSV, open it, stare at rows and columns, get a vague sense things are up or down, close the file. So, the questions that actually matter go unanswered, not because they're unanswerable, but because answering felt too hard. Decisions ride on gut feeling instead. Point Claude at that same file

title: Ask it plainly — no formula required
text: And ask the way you'd ask a colleague, which clients bring in the most revenue and has the mix changed over the last two quarters? No formula, no pivot table. Claude reads the data, runs the analysis, and hands back a sentence you can act on faster than it takes to write a single SUM. That's natural language querying. What were total sales by month? Which client led last quarter? Am I spending more on software than 6 months ago? Claude turns each question into the right analysis and answers in a sentence, not a table of raw numbers.

title: The anchor: three clients, sixty percent, one sliding
text: It turns I think business is going okay into something specific. Three clients carry 60% of revenue and one has been sliding since September. That's the gap between reacting to problems and seeing them coming.

title: Four kinds of work — explore, clean, visualize, compare
text: Beyond answering, there are four kinds of work: exploration, cleaning, visualization, and comparison. Not every question needs all four, but together they turn a raw export into something you can trust and act on. Exploration first. Point Claude at mystery export, column headers that don't quite make sense, and it describes the structure, flags outliers, and suggests the questions worth asking. Often the best question isn't the one you started with. Cleaning. Messy data is the norm. Inconsistent date formats, duplicate rows, impossible values like negative sales. The plugin does this tedious work and reports exactly what it changed. Automate that and the barrier to actually working with your numbers falls away. Visualization, ask for monthly revenue over the past year and you get a chart for a deck, a partner, or just to see your own trajectory. Line charts for trends, bars for comparisons, and you can always ask for something different. In comparison, how does this quarter stack against last? Is acquisition cost climbing or falling? Totals tell you where you are, comparisons tell you where you're heading.

title: The avoided question: am I profitable month to month?
text: Every business has a question it's been avoiding. Start there. Point Claude at your invoices and your expenses and ask, "Am I profitable month to month?" It reads both files, correlates them, and gives you a real read on your financial health.

title: Make it a monthly ritual
text: You'll know more about your finances after this 5-minute conversation than after a year of meaning to look. So, make it a ritual. First of the month, 10 minutes, point Claude at last month's revenue and expenses and ask for health check. Total revenue, total expenses, margin, how it compares to the month before, and anything that looks off. Do it every month and you're never surprised by your own numbers again. Each review stacks on the last until a trend is visible before it becomes a problem.

title: How concentrated is your revenue?
text: For a service business, one question matters most. How concentrated is your revenue? Ask directly, "Who are my top clients? What share rides on the top three? And is anyone quietly spending less than before?" Concentration is one of the most important things a solo operator can know. If a single client is, say, 40% of your income and you don't know it, you can't plan for the day they leave. The plugin makes that check trivial.

title: The anchor returns — caught early
text: And the follow-up is cheap. Of those top clients, which are declining? What changed last quarter that might explain it? The plugin makes each next question almost free, so ask it. Remember the client sliding since September? This is how you'd catch that early.

title: Only as trustworthy as your data and your assumptions
text: Here's the honest part. The plugin's analysis is only as trustworthy as two things: the data you fed it and the assumptions underneath it. Clean inputs and sound assumptions give a reliable read. Bad inputs give confident, well-formatted nonsense. That's exactly why it reports what it cleaned, so you can verify the fixes before trusting the numbers built on top of them. The change log isn't paperwork, it's the audit trail.

title: What it can't tell you
text: The plugin can tell you a client is declining. It can't tell you whether to call them, discount, or let them go. It surfaces the number, you own the decision. Four habits make it sing. Ask a specific question, not analyze my data. Iterate, your first question breeds a better one. Compare, don't just total. And export on a schedule, because the plugin can only work with the data you actually give it. The data plugin turns

title: Carry-out
text: The spreadsheet you're avoiding into a 5-minute conversation, but the answer is only as trustworthy as your data and your assumptions. So, the judgment stays yours.

title: Your turn
text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. Here's a spreadsheet of my invoices and one of my expenses for the year. Tell me what's in each file and flag anything messy. Then, give me a business health check. Am I profitable month-to-month? Which months were strongest and weakest? Is any expense growing faster than revenue?
